title: Creating the DELETE Route
summary: Finishes the joke API with two DELETE routes: remove one joke by id, and wipe the whole collection only when the caller supplies the correct master key as a query parameter, a minimal form of API-key protection.

concepts.heading: Challenge 7: DELETE /jokes/:id
points: Uses Express's app.delete(route, callback). The id arrives as a path variable in req.params.id; convert with parseInt and use ===, or skip the conversion and use ==.
Locate the joke with findIndex, which returns -1 when nothing matches.
If the index is greater than -1, jokes.splice(searchIndex, 1) removes exactly one element starting at that index (splice mutates the array in place), then res.sendStatus(200) replies OK.
Otherwise reply with res.status(404).json({ error: ... }) saying the joke was not found and that nothing was deleted.
A single-joke delete is low risk, so no authentication is applied.
The solution file leaves an optional prompt about edge cases when deleting by id; the missing-id case handled by the 404 branch is the one it points at.

concepts.heading: Challenge 8: DELETE /all with a master key
points: Wiping the whole collection is dangerous, so the route demands a secret key sent as a query parameter named key (e.g. /all?key=<code>). In Postman this is under Params > Query Parameters.
The starter file defines a masterKey constant near the top, representing the secret kept on the server. Later modules cover generating real keys and proper authentication.

Handler: read req.query.key into userKey and compare with masterKey. If equal, reassign the array to an empty array (jokes = []) and send status 200. If not, respond with a 404 status and a JSON error saying the caller is not authorised.
Because the handler reassigns jokes, the array must be declared with var or let rather than const (the reference file uses var).
This is a very simplified key check; it only illustrates guarding risky operations. Real systems add hashed credentials, tokens, HTTPS and so on, which come later in the course.
(Extra) A 401 or 403 status is more conventional than 404 for failed authorisation, and sending secrets in the query string leaves them in logs and browser history.

concepts.heading: Wrap-up
points: Compare your behaviour with solution.js and confirm both DELETE requests in the Postman collection respond as expected. The next lesson applies all of these routes to a blog API.

task.name: DIY API: DELETE routes
task.starting_point: DIY API project with GET, POST, PUT and PATCH done; index.js has slots for challenges 7 and 8 and a masterKey constant near the top; Postman collection has DELETE a Joke and DELETE All Jokes requests.
task.goal: Implement DELETE /jokes/:id to remove one joke and DELETE /all to clear all jokes only when the correct key query parameter is supplied.
steps: Challenge 7: add app.delete('/jokes/:id', ...); parse the id and find its index with findIndex.
If the index exists, splice one element out at that index and respond with status 200; otherwise respond 404 with a JSON error message.
If it equals masterKey, set jokes to an empty array and send status 200; otherwise send an error status with a JSON 'not authorised' message.
Run nodemon index.js and send both DELETE requests from Postman, trying a valid id, an unknown id, a wrong key and the right key; then GET to see the array changed.
task.expected_result: Deleting an existing id returns OK 200 and that joke disappears; an unknown id returns a 404 JSON error; /all with the right key returns 200 and leaves an empty collection; a wrong or missing key returns the error and deletes nothing.
task.reference_repo_path: Section 30 - Build Your Own API/30.02 DIY API/solution.js

pitfalls: Calling splice(-1, 1) when findIndex returns -1 would delete the last joke; always check the index is greater than -1 first.
Declaring the jokes array with const and then trying to reassign it to [] in the delete-all route.
Leaving the key check out so anyone can wipe the data.
(Extra) Hard-coding a secret in source; the course does this only for teaching.

gaps_and_ideas: New lesson 'DELETE routes and simple API-key protection' with a blurb on removing resources and guarding destructive endpoints.

Tasks: (1) delete one item by id using findIndex and splice, (2) return a 404 JSON error for an unknown id, (3) add a /all route requiring ?key=, (4) (Extra) move the key to an environment variable, (5) (Extra) use 401/403 for bad keys.
Starter code idea: Express app with an items array and a secret constant.
Interactive demo idea: a visual array where the learner sends DELETE requests with different ids and keys and sees elements vanish or the error response.
